newsitem.title: USA: Army culture led to sex-scandal, retired major says.
newsitem.headline: Army culture led to sex-scandal, retired major says.

text.p: Army culture and the prohibition on women soldiers taking part in direct ground combat are factors behind the sexual harassment scandal that erupted recently, a retired female Army major said Sunday.

"The Army still has a very, very male-dominated culture. The purpose of the Army is to engage in direct ground combat and thus the whole culture is oriented towards that goal, as it really should be," retired Maj. Lillian Pfluke said in a television interview.
"But the problem is that women are still totally excluded from any position that engages in direct ground combat," she told ABC Television's "This Week."

"Any time you have two castes of people you're going to have some kind of tensions. You have some people thinking they're superior to the others, some people think they can't contribute as much as they would like to, and I think that really is the root cause of the whole thing," she said.
The Army on Friday launched a high-level investigation of the sex scandal, including whether any top officers should be held responsible for the rape and harassment of female recruits.

Since the scandal broke two weeks ago, at least 10 drill instructors and other trainers have been charged with violations ranging from rape to "fraternizing" with female recruits at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland and and at Fort Leonard Wood in Missouri.

"The Army really does have on paper an excellent sexual harrassment complaint processing programme," Pfluke said. "The problem is that the culture hasn't come as far yet to really implement that," she added.
"If you had women as equal members of the team. If you treated all soldiers as soldiers, not as women soldiers and men soldiers ... a lot of that would be eradicated," Pfluke said.

Army Secretary Togo West said he has discussed the situation with Defence Secretary William Perry and that the message he received was very clear -- "get to the bottom of it and remember we will not tolerate that in our armed forces."

Army officials were surprised by the number of calls received by a newly established sexual abuse hotline, West said on the same television programme. The hotline has received 5,000 calls of which 700 were being investigated further, he said.
Since the scandal broke at Aberdeen, the Army has begun investigating possible harassment of young recruits at all of its training bases.
